newsitem.title: CANADA: Chretien mulls Canada cabinet, Martin seen staying.
newsitem.headline: Chretien mulls Canada cabinet, Martin seen staying.

text.p: Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien explored possible choices for his new cabinet on Monday, confident he would reap the benefits in his second term of the government's recent fiscal discipline.
"We're beginning a new mandate in an extremely good position," Chretien told a cheering caucus of Liberal legislators at their first gathering since his re-election last Monday.
"We have a majority government, and I do think the sacrifices that we have asked the Canadian people to make in the last four years will pay a lot of dividends, because we have done the right thing."
Chretien was due to name his new cabinet on Wednesday morning, and government sources said he had not finished talking to all the prospective cabinet choices.
But he was expected to make a sweeping shuffle, with Finance Minister Paul Martin and Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy among the few likely to stay put.

Martin's position, as the person responsible for restoring Canada's international fiscal respectability and holding the purse strings for the whole government, is the most important for setting the overall economic direction of the government.
"I wouldn't believe he is going anywhere," one source said. "He won't have to move his boxes, I don't think."

Watching the future of Deputy Prime Minister Sheila Copps, on the left wing of the party, may give a hint of the direction of the party as it emerges from battling deficits to deciding what to do with possible fiscal surpluses.

Chretien, Copps and Martin all fought for the leadership of the Liberal Party in 1990 -- which Chretien won -- but Copps had been to a large extent marginalized over the past three years as the party swung to the fiscal right.

The sources said it appeared clear she would give up deputy prime minister, but it was uncertain if she would stay on as minister of Canadian heritage -- where she has defended cultural protection -- or possibly move to health, expected to be a juicy portfolio if new money is freed up.

Chretien faces the difficult task of balancing demands for representation from Canada's regions with the fact that his caucus is two-thirds from Ontario, which obviously cannot get that proportion of cabinet posts.
The West is particularly sensitive to the idea of what might happen to agriculture and natural resources.

Two from rural Ontario have been mentioned as candidates for those portfolios, both of which chaired House of Commons committees in those areas and would be seen to stay the course -- Lyle Vanclief and Andy Mitchell, respectively.
And he must decide whether to swing left to prevent further losses in impoverished Atlantic Canada or worry about the West, where the right-wing Reform Party won most seats.

"To be a Liberal these days is easy, the definition is: the people on the right will say that you're on the left and the people on the left will say that you're on the right," he quipped. "So you know where you are, you're right in the middle, the radical centre."
